title: Area Decomposition
coreInsight: Area is additive and preserved under valid cut-and-rearrange operations, so complicated figures can be replaced by simpler equivalent pieces.
targetLearnerRealization: A complicated region can be partitioned, completed, or subtracted using familiar areas, provided every point is counted exactly once.
learningObjectives: Enclose and subtract missing regions from a familiar whole.
Partition a region into non-overlapping familiar shapes.
Justify that a decomposition has complete coverage and no overlap.
Distinguish measured or marked congruence from visual resemblance.
Use fractional corner areas to find a central region.

continuity.openingCallback: Use rectangle, square, and triangle area as trusted building blocks for a region with no single formula.
closingSeeds: The same cut-and-rearrange principle can compare curved, coordinate, and similar regions.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Pieces may overlap or leave gaps without changing the total.
Regions that look congruent are automatically congruent.
Removed regions should sometimes be added rather than subtracted.
Equal-looking regions are necessarily equal in area.

beats.purpose: Create decomposition as the necessary idea through an authentic region with no special formula.
beats.expectedRealization: The shaded area is the outer 5-by-5 square minus all three unshaded squares.
beats.transitionIn: An L-shaped floor has no formula to memorize. Surround it with a familiar whole and track exactly what is missing.
beats.whyNow: This authentic diagram isolates area additivity and immediately supports more than one valid decomposition.
beats.entryBridge: Find the outer side length before calculating any area, then identify every region not shaded.
beats.exitBridge: The whole area 25 splits into shaded 14 plus three white squares totaling 11.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Translucent area pieces inside one enclosing square.
learnerPrompts: What familiar shape contains the entire region?
What goes wrong if one white square is missed?
What is the total area of all three removed squares?
Why does whole minus removed equal the shaded area?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The outer area is 25 and the three removed areas total 11, leaving 14.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Build the outer side as 1 + 3 + 1, then subtract every unshaded square exactly once.

steps.title: Build the whole
steps.body: The outer square has side 1 + 3 + 1 = 5 and area 25.

steps.title: Account for every hole
steps.body: The white squares have areas 1², 3², and 1², totaling 11.

resolution.takeaway: Enclose an awkward region in a familiar whole, then subtract every missing part exactly once.

beats.purpose: State the coverage and non-overlap conditions that make area addition valid.
beats.expectedRealization: A partition proves an area sum only when its pieces exactly cover the target with disjoint interiors.
beats.transitionIn: The subtraction worked because shaded and white regions accounted for the whole square without double counting.
beats.prompt: Which condition makes an area decomposition valid?

options.text: The pieces cover the target completely and their interiors do not overlap.
The pieces look about the same size.
The plan uses at least three pieces.
Every piece uses the same area formula.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Complete coverage and no overlap make the piece areas add to the target.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask whether every point of the target is counted once—not zero times or twice.

steps.title: Check coverage
steps.body: Every point in the target must lie in at least one chosen piece.

steps.title: Check non-overlap
steps.body: No interior point may lie in two pieces, or its area would be counted twice.

resolution.takeaway: A valid partition counts every bit of area exactly once.

beats.purpose: Compare addition and subtraction as equivalent valid routes.
beats.expectedRealization: Different decompositions agree because they account for the same target region exactly once.
beats.transitionIn: The L-shape can also be split into rectangles instead of carved from a square.
beats.prompt: One method subtracts holes from a 25-unit square. Another splits the shaded L into rectangles of areas 5 and 9. Why must both totals agree?

options.text: Both account for exactly the same shaded points once.
The methods use the same perimeter.
Different decompositions agree only by coincidence.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Area depends on the covered set, not on which valid cuts describe it.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare what region each method covers, not the number or shape of its pieces.

visual.ariaLabel: Two valid decompositions of the same shaded region both totaling fourteen square units

steps.body: Both methods cover every shaded point once and no white point, so both compute the same area: 14.

resolution.takeaway: Valid decompositions may look different but must preserve total coverage.

beats.purpose: Name the technique after its invariant and validity conditions are understood.
beats.expectedRealization: Partition, subtraction, and rearrangement are versions of the same additive principle.
beats.name: Area decomposition
beats.conciseDefinition: Replace a complicated region by non-overlapping familiar pieces, or by a familiar whole minus missing pieces. A cut-and-rearrange preserves area when no piece is stretched, duplicated, overlapped, or lost.
beats.formalization: area(whole) = sum of disjoint piece areas · area(target) = area(container) − area(complement)
beats.memoryHook: Cover once: cut and add, or enclose and subtract.

beats.purpose: Transfer subtraction to fractional corner triangles when direct dimensions are unavailable.
beats.expectedRealization: The central triangle is the rectangle minus three disjoint corner triangles totaling 5/8 of the whole.
beats.transitionIn: The L-shape removed squares with known side lengths. Now remove corner triangles whose areas are known only as fractions of a rectangle.
beats.whyNow: The learner can audit coverage and non-overlap, so midpoint information can determine relative area without inventing side lengths.
beats.entryBridge: Treat the rectangle's area as one whole, find each corner triangle's fraction, then subtract.
beats.exitBridge: The corners total 5/8, leaving 3/8 of 72, or 27.
beats.reusedRepresentation: One container partitioned into translucent target and complement pieces.
learnerPrompts: Which triangle is the target inside the rectangle?
What fractions of the rectangle are the three corner triangles?
Do those corners overlap or leave any outside region uncounted?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The target is 3/8 of 72, which is 27.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Subtract the three corner triangles: their fractions are 1/4, 1/8, and 1/4 of the rectangle.

steps.title: Measure corners by fractions
steps.body: The three right-triangle corners occupy 1/4, 1/8, and 1/4 of the rectangle.

steps.title: Audit the complement
steps.body: They have disjoint interiors and together form exactly the region outside the central triangle, totaling 5/8.

steps.title: Take the remainder
steps.body: The target is 1 − 5/8 = 3/8 of the rectangle, and (3/8) × 72 = 27.

resolution.takeaway: Relative area can replace missing dimensions when a partition's fractions are controlled.

beats.purpose: Assess rectangular partition of an L-shape.
beats.whyNow: Return to addition rather than outer subtraction.
beats.entryBridge: Split along the inside corner into two non-overlapping rectangles.
learnerPrompts: Where can one cut create two rectangles with no overlap?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The two rectangular pieces total 34 square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Split the L into a 6-by-4 rectangle and a 5-by-2 rectangle.

resolution.takeaway: A clean cut can replace an unfamiliar outline with familiar pieces.

beats.whyNow: Switch from addition to an explicitly removed region.
beats.entryBridge: Compute the outer coverage and subtract the inner opening.
learnerPrompts: Which region is absent and must be subtracted?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The frame covers 72 square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The opening is not material; subtract its area from the outer rectangle.

steps.body: Outer area 12 × 8 = 96. Opening area 6 × 4 = 24. Frame area 96 − 24 = 72.

resolution.takeaway: A hole is removed coverage, so subtract it.

beats.purpose: Assess correction for overlapping area descriptions.
beats.whyNow: Make double counting explicit in a union of rectangles.
beats.entryBridge: Add both rectangle areas, then inspect the shared square.
beats.exitBridge: Subtract the 4-square overlap once to get 35.
learnerPrompts: Which points were included in both initial products?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The union area is 35 square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The overlapping 2-by-2 square was counted in both rectangle areas; remove one copy.

steps.body: The rectangles contribute 6 × 4 + 5 × 3 = 39, but their 2 × 2 overlap was counted twice. Subtract one overlap: 39 − 4 = 35.

resolution.takeaway: When added pieces overlap, subtract the duplicated coverage once.

beats.purpose: Assess whether visual resemblance is sufficient to claim equal area.
beats.whyNow: Test the evidence required for area-preserving rearrangement.
beats.entryBridge: Look for measurements or a rigid-motion relationship.
learnerPrompts: What exact fact proves the pieces have equal dimensions?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The areas cannot be proven equal from appearance alone.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A not-to-scale sketch cannot replace equal-length marks or measurements.

steps.body: Without matching dimensions, congruence marks, or a rigid-motion argument, the two regions may have different areas despite looking alike.

resolution.takeaway: Area equality needs structural evidence, not visual similarity.

beats.whyNow: Finish with a cut whose pieces are justified congruent by a rectangle's diagonal.
beats.entryBridge: Use the 180° rotation that swaps the two diagonal pieces.
beats.exitBridge: Each triangle is half of area 70, so 35.
learnerPrompts: Why are the two pieces equal rather than merely equal-looking?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The diagonal creates two congruent triangles, each area 35.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A rectangle's diagonal divides it into two triangles that match under a half-turn.

steps.body: The 10-by-7 rectangle has area 70. Its diagonal makes two congruent triangles, so each has area 70 ÷ 2 = 35.

resolution.takeaway: A proven congruence can justify an equal-area split.

beats.purpose: Consolidate route choice and exact coverage auditing.
beats.expectedRealization: A decomposition is valid because of coverage accounting, not because its arithmetic happens to work.
beats.transitionIn: L-shapes, frames, overlapping rectangles, corner triangles, and diagonal halves all required an exact account of where area went.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable decomposition routine? Select all four.

options.text: Choose disjoint pieces or a container and complement.
Justify equal pieces with measurements or a valid motion.
Check every target point is counted exactly once.

response.feedback: Each action protects the area invariant.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Mark, choose, justify, and audit before totaling.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four are required; arithmetic cannot repair an invalid partition.

steps.body: A correct total follows from a correct partition: complete coverage, disjoint interiors, and justified dimensions.

resolution.takeaway: Cut strategically, but prove the accounting.

beats.purpose: Consolidate flexible strategy selection without inventing a successor.
beats.expectedRealization: Addition, subtraction, and rearrangement are interchangeable only when their coverage claims are proved.
beats.transitionIn: The same region may invite several calculations, but they all answer one coverage question.
beats.prompt: When would enclosing and subtracting be cleaner than cutting and adding—and what audit must either method pass?
beats.takeaway: Choose the simplest shapes, then verify that the target is covered once and only once.

notes: Design: the authentic L-shaped region is the discovery anchor. Its enclosing-square subtraction leads immediately to the completeness/non-overlap invariant and an alternative additive partition. The midpoint-triangle transfer replaces absolute dimensions with fractional complement areas.

Beat outline: authentic L-shape anchor -> coverage audit -> compare valid routes -> name decomposition -> authentic midpoint transfer -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> strategy reflection.
Both mapped animations are referenced unchanged after submission over their full timelines. Existing choice-grid visuals suffice; no renderer or animation source changes were made.

Generated answers were recomputed through disjoint sums, container-minus-hole subtraction, overlap correction, and congruent halves, with independent reverse totals, rigid-motion evidence, or option audits. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
